title: Gabapentin and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink? Risks and Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on gabapentin? How gabapentin and alcohol stack up in your brain, the FDA breathing warning, how long to wait, and the emergency signs to know.
metaDescription: Can you drink on gabapentin? How gabapentin and alcohol interact, the FDA breathing warning, how long to wait, and the warning signs that need help fast.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** gabapentin and alcohol both slow down your brain and nervous system, and when you take them together the effects add up. That means more drowsiness, more dizziness, worse coordination, slower reactions, and, in the wrong circumstances, slowed breathing. The label for Neurontin (brand-name gabapentin) tells people not to drink alcohol while taking it without first talking to their healthcare provider. For a healthy person on a low dose, a single drink may not cause a crisis, but you can't predict how strongly the two will hit you on a given night, and the risk climbs quickly with more drinks, higher doses, and any other sedating medicine in the mix.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on gabapentin unless your prescriber has told you it's okay for your situation. Never combine gabapentin and alcohol with opioids, benzodiazepines (like Xanax or Valium), sleeping pills, or sedating antihistamines. Don't drive or do anything risky after mixing them. Don't skip or stop your gabapentin to "make room" for drinking, because stopping suddenly can cause its own problems. And if someone who has mixed them is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly or shallowly, or has blue or gray lips, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how gabapentin and alcohol interact and what the official guidance says. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your dose, your other medicines, and your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking if** you take gabapentin (Neurontin, Gralise, or Horizant) or pregabalin (Lyrica), especially if you also take an opioid, an anxiety or sleep medicine, or an antihistamine, or if you have lung disease, kidney disease, or are over 65. **Call 911 right away if** someone who has taken gabapentin and alcohol is extremely sleepy or can't be woken, is confused, has slow, shallow, or noisy breathing, or has bluish lips or fingertips. For questions about a possible overdose, US readers can call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222**.

## What Gabapentin Is and How It Works

Gabapentin is a prescription medicine first approved to help control certain seizures and to treat nerve pain after shingles (postherpetic neuralgia). Brand names include **Neurontin**, **Gralise** (a once-daily version), and **Horizant** (gabapentin enacarbil, an extended-release form also used for restless legs syndrome). Doctors also prescribe gabapentin "off-label," meaning for uses outside the official approval, such as other kinds of nerve pain, hot flashes, sleep problems, and anxiety. Because it's so widely prescribed, a lot of people take it who would never think of themselves as being on a "serious" drug.

Despite the name, gabapentin doesn't work by acting directly on GABA, the brain's main calming chemical. Instead, it attaches to a part of certain calcium channels on nerve cells (called the alpha-2-delta subunit). This turns down the release of the chemical messengers that make nerves fire. The result is calmer, quieter nerve signaling, which is why it helps with seizures and with pain from overactive nerves.

That same calming effect is also behind its most common side effects: sleepiness, dizziness, feeling unsteady on your feet, fatigue, and sometimes blurry vision or trouble concentrating. These are often strongest when you first start the medicine or when your dose goes up.

A few other facts matter for drinking:

- **Your liver doesn't break gabapentin down.** It leaves the body mostly unchanged through the kidneys. So unlike Tylenol, the main worry with alcohol isn't liver damage. It's the combined effect on your brain and breathing.
- **It doesn't last very long.** For people with normal kidney function, gabapentin's half-life (the time it takes for the amount in your body to drop by half) is roughly five to seven hours. That's why it's usually taken two or three times a day. People with reduced kidney function clear it much more slowly.
- **Pregabalin (Lyrica) is a close cousin.** It works the same way, carries the same kind of warnings, and everything in this article about alcohol applies to it as well.

## Why Gabapentin and Alcohol Don't Mix

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It boosts the brain's calming signals and blocks some of its excitatory ones, which is why a drink or two makes you relaxed and a lot of drinks make you clumsy, slurring, and sleepy. Gabapentin quiets nerve signaling through a different route. When you combine two things that slow the brain down by different routes, you don't get one or the other. You get both stacked together.

In practice, that stacking shows up in a few ways:

1. **More sedation than you expect.** Drinks you normally handle can leave you much drowsier, foggier, or more "out of it" than usual. People sometimes describe feeling drunk after one or two drinks.
2. **Worse balance and coordination.** Both substances cause dizziness and unsteadiness on their own. Together they raise the risk of falls and injuries, which is a particular concern for older adults.
3. **Slower thinking and reactions.** Judgment, memory, and reaction time all take a bigger hit, which makes driving or operating anything dangerous a real hazard.
4. **Slowed breathing.** This is the most serious risk. At higher amounts, or when other sedating drugs are involved, the combined depressant effect can suppress the brain's drive to breathe.

### The FDA's breathing warning

In December 2019, the US Food and Drug Administration issued a safety communication warning that gabapentin and pregabalin can cause serious breathing problems in people who have respiratory risk factors. The FDA listed those risk factors as using opioids or other drugs that depress the central nervous system, having a condition that reduces lung function such as COPD, and being elderly. It required new warnings about this risk on the labels of these medicines.

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant, so it falls squarely into the "other drugs that depress the central nervous system" group. The FDA's warning wasn't about one drink with dinner in a healthy 30-year-old. It was about the situations where breathing problems are most likely: several depressants at once, lung disease, and older age. But it's the clearest official signal that mixing gabapentin with other sedating substances isn't a harmless shortcut.

### Why "it's not a controlled substance" is misleading

Gabapentin isn't a federally controlled substance in the US, and many people assume that means it's mild. It's true that on its own, at prescribed doses, gabapentin has a fairly good safety record. The danger comes from combinations. Public health researchers, including the CDC, have reported that gabapentin frequently shows up alongside opioids in overdose deaths. Gabapentin is rarely the only drug involved; it's the stacking that's dangerous. Some US states have added gabapentin to their prescription monitoring programs or scheduled it locally because of this pattern.

The lesson for anyone who drinks: the more sedating things you add together, whether that's alcohol, gabapentin, opioid painkillers, anxiety medicines, sleep aids, or cannabis, the less predictable and more dangerous the result.

## Can You Have One Drink on Gabapentin?

This is the question most people are really asking, and the honest answer is: it depends on you, and it's a question for your prescriber, not the internet.

The official position is simple. The Neurontin medication guide tells patients not to drink alcohol or take other medicines that make them sleepy or dizzy while on gabapentin without first talking with their healthcare provider. That isn't a flat ban in every case, but it does mean the default is "don't, unless your doctor says it's okay."

In real life, doctors weigh things like:

- **Your dose.** Someone on a small dose at bedtime is in a different position from someone taking a high dose three times a day.
- **How long you've been on it.** Side effects like drowsiness and dizziness are usually worst in the first weeks and after dose increases.
- **Your other medicines.** An opioid, benzodiazepine, muscle relaxant, sleep medicine, or sedating antihistamine changes the picture a lot.
- **Your age, lungs, and kidneys.** Older adults, people with COPD or sleep apnea, and people with reduced kidney function are at higher risk.
- **Why you take it.** If gabapentin controls seizures, alcohol and the poor sleep that often follows a night of drinking can make seizures more likely on their own.

If your prescriber has said an occasional drink is okay for you, sensible guardrails include: have one drink rather than several, have it with food, sip it slowly, don't drink close to a dose when the medicine is at its strongest, stay somewhere safe, and don't drive. Pay attention to how you feel. If one drink hits you noticeably harder than normal, that's your body telling you the combination is strong for you.

If you haven't asked, the safest choice is not to drink until you do. The question takes thirty seconds at the pharmacy counter.

## How Long After Gabapentin Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period, and you'll see a lot of confident numbers online that aren't backed by anything. Here's what's actually useful to know.

Gabapentin's effect builds up after each dose. With a half-life of roughly five to seven hours in people with healthy kidneys, a meaningful amount stays in your system for well over a day after your last dose. If you take it on a regular schedule, which most people do, there is never really a point between doses when it's "out" of your system. That's why waiting a few hours after a pill doesn't make the combination safe, and why the label advice is about the whole time you're on the medicine, not just the hours right after a dose.

Two related points matter just as much:

- **Don't skip or stop doses so you can drink.** Stopping gabapentin suddenly, especially after taking it for a while or at higher doses, can cause withdrawal-type symptoms such as anxiety, trouble sleeping, sweating, nausea, and pain. In people who take it for epilepsy, stopping abruptly can trigger seizures. The label says to lower the dose gradually under a doctor's guidance. Skipping doses around a weekend of drinking is a bad trade.
- **Kidney function changes the timeline.** If your kidneys don't work at full strength, gabapentin builds up and stays longer. Your doctor may already have you on a lower dose for that reason.

If you've stopped gabapentin for good under your doctor's direction, ask them when it's reasonable to drink again. For most people with normal kidneys, the drug is essentially gone within a couple of days of the last dose, but your doctor can give you an answer based on your dose and health.

## Extended-Release Gabapentin and Alcohol

Gralise and Horizant are designed to release medicine slowly over the day. Alcohol can sometimes change how extended-release products behave in the body, and the labels for these versions include their own specific guidance about alcohol. If you take an extended-release form, check the medication guide that came with your prescription or ask your pharmacist exactly what it says. Don't assume the advice is identical to regular gabapentin.

## Gabapentin, Alcohol, and the Next-Day Hangover

Mixing the two can make the morning after worse in a few predictable ways.

- **More grogginess.** Both alcohol and gabapentin can leave you foggy. Together, the "heavy head" feeling can last longer into the next day.
- **More dizziness and unsteadiness.** Hangover dizziness plus gabapentin dizziness raises the risk of falls, especially getting out of bed or the shower.
- **Poorer sleep.** Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster but breaks up sleep later in the night. Gabapentin can change sleep patterns too. You may feel like you slept a long time and still wake up tired. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what alcohol does to sleep.

### What not to do the morning after

- **Don't take extra gabapentin** for the headache or the shakiness. Stick to your prescribed dose and schedule.
- **Don't stack sleep aids** to "catch up" on rest. Diphenhydramine (the antihistamine in Benadryl, ZzzQuil, and many "PM" products) and doxylamine add more sedation on top of gabapentin. See our guides to [ZzzQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/zzzquil-and-alcohol) and [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) for why those are poor choices after drinking.
- **Watch your antacid timing.** The Neurontin label notes that antacids containing aluminum and magnesium hydroxide (such as Maalox) reduce how much gabapentin you absorb, and it advises taking gabapentin at least two hours after that kind of antacid. If you reach for one for an upset stomach, space it from your dose. For more on stomach remedies, see our guide on [Tums and alcohol](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol).

For a hangover headache, gabapentin doesn't have a known significant interaction with standard doses of acetaminophen or ibuprofen, but each of those carries its own alcohol warning. Ask your pharmacist which is the better choice for you, and stick to the label dose.

## What Else Makes the Combination More Dangerous

The risk from gabapentin and alcohol rises sharply when a third sedating substance joins in. Be especially careful with:

- **Opioid painkillers** such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, tramadol, or morphine. This is the combination the FDA flagged most strongly. Gabapentin is often prescribed alongside opioids for pain, so this situation is common.
- **Benzodiazepines** such as alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan), clonazepam (Klonopin), or diazepam (Valium).
- **Sleep medicines** such as zolpidem (Ambien) or eszopiclone (Lunesta).
- **Sedating antihistamines** like diphenhydramine and doxylamine, including nighttime cold and flu products.
- **Muscle relaxants** like cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril) or methocarbamol.
- **Some antidepressants and antipsychotics** that cause drowsiness.
- **Cannabis**, which adds its own sedation and dizziness.

If you take gabapentin plus any of these, alcohol is a much bigger deal, and you should get specific advice from your doctor or pharmacist before you drink at all. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers more common medicine and supplement combinations.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Most of the time, mixing a modest amount of alcohol with gabapentin leads to feeling unusually drowsy and unsteady. That's unpleasant and makes accidents more likely, but it passes. The signs below are different. They point to dangerous sedation or breathing problems, and they need emergency care.

**Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has taken gabapentin and alcohol:**

- Is very hard to wake up, or can't be woken
- Has slow, shallow, irregular, or noisy breathing (snoring or gurgling sounds in someone you can't rouse)
- Has blue, gray, or pale lips or fingertips
- Is severely confused, can't speak clearly, or is acting very out of character
- Has a seizure
- Has also taken opioids, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives and is very drowsy

While you wait for help, stay with the person, keep them on their side so they don't choke if they vomit, and don't let them "sleep it off" alone. If opioids might be involved and naloxone (Narcan) is available, it's reasonable to give it; it won't reverse gabapentin or alcohol, but it can reverse the opioid part, and it won't harm someone who hasn't taken opioids.

**Call your doctor soon (not an emergency, but don't ignore it) if you notice:**

- Ongoing dizziness, unsteadiness, or falls since starting gabapentin
- Feeling so sleepy during the day that it's affecting work or driving
- New or worsening mood changes, including depression or thoughts of self-harm. Antiepileptic medicines, including gabapentin, carry a label warning about this, and alcohol can make low moods worse.
- Swelling in your hands, feet, or legs, or a skin rash

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Some people should treat any drinking on gabapentin as a conversation that must happen with their doctor first:

- **Anyone also taking opioids, benzodiazepines, or sleep medicines.**
- **People over 65.** Older adults are more sensitive to sedation and more likely to fall, and the FDA named older age as a risk factor for breathing problems.
- **People with COPD, asthma, sleep apnea, or other lung or breathing conditions.**
- **People with kidney disease**, who clear gabapentin more slowly.
- **People who take gabapentin for seizures**, since alcohol and disrupted sleep can both lower the seizure threshold.
- **Anyone who drives for work, operates machinery, or cares for young children.**

## A Note on Gabapentin for Cutting Back on Drinking

Some doctors prescribe gabapentin as part of a plan to help people reduce how much they drink, and it has been studied for that purpose. If that's why you take it, your prescriber has given you instructions that fit your situation, and those come first. This article is written for people who take gabapentin for pain, sleep, nerve symptoms, or other reasons and want to know whether they can have a drink. Either way, the same safety signs apply.

If you notice that you keep looking for ways to drink while on a medicine that warns against it, that's worth mentioning to your doctor too. It's a normal, useful thing to bring up, and they'd rather know.

## Practical Tips if Your Doctor Says a Drink Is Okay

If you've had the conversation and your prescriber is comfortable with occasional, light drinking, these habits keep the risk low:

1. **Try it first at home**, not at a party or before you need to drive. See how a single drink feels on your current dose.
2. **Keep it to one or two drinks** and sip slowly. Standard drinks are smaller than many people pour: about 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits.
3. **Eat before and while you drink**, and drink water alongside.
4. **Never drive** after combining them, even if you feel fine. Reaction time can be off before you notice it.
5. **Tell someone you're with** that you take a medicine that makes alcohol hit harder.
6. **Skip the nightcap and sleep aids.** Don't add a sedating antihistamine or sleep medicine to the mix.
7. **Recheck after any dose change.** If your gabapentin dose goes up, assume alcohol will affect you more until you know otherwise.

For general habits that make any night of drinking easier on your body, our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the strategies with the best evidence.

## What About DHM and Other Hangover Supplements?

People who take gabapentin sometimes ask whether a hangover supplement like DHM (dihydromyricetin) is safe to use. The honest answer is that nobody has studied DHM together with gabapentin in people, so there is no good evidence either way about how they interact.

What we do know: gabapentin is handled by the kidneys rather than the liver enzymes that process most drugs, so a classic liver-enzyme interaction seems less likely. But DHM's best-studied effect, mostly in animal research, involves the brain's GABA-A receptors, the same calming system alcohol acts on. Anything that works on the brain's calming systems is worth clearing with your doctor before you combine it with a sedating prescription. And no supplement makes it safe to drink on gabapentin, or protects your breathing if you mix sedatives.

If your doctor is comfortable with you using DHM, it's best thought of as a modest helper for occasional social drinking, not a safety net. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

Gabapentin and alcohol both slow the brain down, and together they slow it down more. The usual result is stronger drowsiness, dizziness, and clumsiness, which makes falls, accidents, and bad decisions more likely. The serious risk is slowed breathing, which the FDA has warned about, and which is most likely when opioids, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives are also involved, or in older adults and people with lung disease.

The label guidance is to avoid alcohol unless your healthcare provider has said it's okay. Don't skip doses to drink, don't drive after mixing them, never add other sedatives, and know the emergency signs: someone who can't be woken, is breathing slowly or shallowly, or has blue lips needs 911 right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking gabapentin?**

The official guidance is not to, unless your healthcare provider says it's okay for you. The Neurontin medication guide tells patients not to drink alcohol while taking gabapentin without first talking to their provider. Both substances slow the nervous system, so together they increase drowsiness, dizziness, and impaired coordination, and in some situations can slow breathing.

**What happens if you mix gabapentin and alcohol?**

Most commonly, you feel much drowsier, dizzier, and less coordinated than you would from either one alone, and your judgment and reaction time get worse. This raises the risk of falls and accidents. At higher amounts, or with opioids or other sedatives, the combination can slow breathing to a dangerous degree. Very hard-to-wake sleepiness, slow or shallow breathing, or blue lips are emergencies that need 911.

**How long after taking gabapentin can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period. Gabapentin's half-life is roughly five to seven hours in people with healthy kidneys, so a meaningful amount stays in your body for more than a day after your last dose, and if you take it regularly it never fully clears between doses. Don't skip or stop doses to make room for drinking, because stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms or seizures. Ask your prescriber what's reasonable for you.

**Can gabapentin and alcohol kill you?**

It can be dangerous, though deaths usually involve more than these two. The FDA warned in 2019 that gabapentin and pregabalin can cause serious breathing problems in people who also take opioids or other central nervous system depressants, have lung disease, or are older. Public health reports have found gabapentin often present alongside opioids in overdose deaths. The more sedating substances are combined, the higher the risk.

**Is one beer okay on gabapentin?**

For some people on low doses, a prescriber may say an occasional single drink is acceptable. But that's a judgment for your doctor, based on your dose, other medicines, age, and health. If you haven't asked, the safer choice is not to drink. If you've been told it's okay, have it with food, go slowly, don't drive, and notice whether it hits harder than usual.

**Does gabapentin make a hangover worse?**

It can. Both alcohol and gabapentin cause grogginess and dizziness, so the next morning you may feel foggier and more unsteady than usual. Don't take extra gabapentin or add sleep aids to cope. Rest, eat, drink water, and if you use a pain reliever, check the label and ask a pharmacist which is right for you.

**Is pregabalin (Lyrica) with alcohol the same as gabapentin with alcohol?**

Yes, the concerns are essentially the same. Pregabalin works the same way as gabapentin and was included in the same 2019 FDA breathing warning. Mixing it with alcohol adds sedation, dizziness, and impaired coordination, and it carries the same extra risk with opioids and other sedatives. Ask your doctor before drinking on either one.

**Can I take DHM if I'm on gabapentin?**

There's no good evidence about how DHM and gabapentin interact, because the combination hasn't been studied in people. DHM appears to act on the brain's GABA-A calming system in animal research, so it's worth asking your doctor or pharmacist before combining it with a sedating prescription. DHM does not make it safe to drink on gabapentin.
